prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall state in spin-orbit-coupled materials, and the experimental observation of its protected edge-channel transport in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B051 to B047, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. My first-round reason for putting twisted bilayer graphene first was that it is a concrete prediction followed by an experimental discovery. Topological insulators have the same structure and are older. Kane and Mele showed that time-reversal-invariant insulators with spin-orbit coupling fall into two classes labelled by a Z2 invariant, with protected edge states as the measurable consequence. Molenkamp's group then observed the edge channels in HgTe wells. Fifteen years or more of confirmation in many materials has left the interpretation stable. This is new physics in the sense I care about, a new way of classifying phases, not a refinement of a measurement. Seven of eight members ranked the candidate, and all three B047 supporters give the same core trio. The round-1 exchange has narrowed the objections that kept me from this candidate to the margin of the credit and to the 2016 overlap, and I find the remaining points answerable by citation wording.
statement.case_against: The credit is still not complete. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group tested, and Zhang cannot be recognised. Hasan's three-dimensional observations and the Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents work sit outside a three-name cap. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions is nearby, and a reader will ask whether this is a continuation. The citation must therefore say plainly that it concerns the Z2 invariant and the time-reversal-symmetric edge physics of spin-orbit insulators, not the integer quantum Hall invariant or the Haldane-type transitions honoured in 2016. If the committee decides it cannot defend that distinction, I would go to B051 rather than B010.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B047 is a conceptual reclassification of insulators by a topological invariant instead of a broken symmetry, that it is a complete prediction-then-observation story, and that Mele cannot be dropped because the Kane-Mele papers are joint.
responses.response: I now agree with him on the weight and on the names. In round 1 I leaned toward replacing Mele with Hasan. I accept his and Johansson's argument that the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall paper are joint work of Kane and Mele, so removing Mele would split a single result. Hasan's three-dimensional observation is a real second chapter, but it is a different discovery and can be left to a later prize without weakening this one. The unresolved point we share is Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. A three-name cap cannot hold them, and I think the citation should name the observation of the edge channels in HgTe wells, so that Molenkamp is credited for what he showed and no one is implied to have proposed the material.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first for the clean two-name credit, the 1e-18 performance beyond the caesium definition and the timeliness of the pending redefinition of the second, and he is willing to see the citation framed around the magic-wavelength lattice.
responses.response: The chair asked whether the magic-wavelength framing answers my novelty objection. It narrows it but does not remove it. The lattice scheme is a real idea and the credit is the cleanest on the list. Even so, the cold-atom and comb toolbox was recognised in 1997, 2005 and 2012, and the strongest consequences Kroll lists, the redefinition, geodesy and tests of constants, are still prospective. I also accept his answer that the science does not depend on the redefinition. My weighing is that a new classification of matter with a confirmed experimental realisation outranks a very large step in precision for an existing instrument. That is a judgement about type of achievement, and I do not hold that it alone must decide the matter, since Kroll and Lindroth could fairly weigh it the other way. I would not oppose B010 and I list it as an alternative. I note Kroll's possible Boulder connection and think it is for him and the chair to judge.

responses.point: Olsson raises whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before honouring lattice clocks, and lists the 2016 topological prize as a risk for B047.
responses.response: On the redefinition, I agree with Kroll and Lindroth that the science does not depend on it, and I would not use it as a reason to postpone. On 2016, which Olsson and Kroll cite as a risk, my view is that the overlap is narrower than it looks. The 2016 prize concerned topological invariants of integer quantum Hall states and the Kosterlitz-Thouless and Haldane transitions, where the invariant arises from broken time reversal or a magnetic field. The Z2 invariant protects edge states by time-reversal symmetry in a spin-orbit band structure, with no magnetic field, and Molenkamp measured them. I do not claim to settle this for her, since the question is what a reader of the citation will see.

responses.point: Eriksson describes B047 as stable after fifteen to twenty years, prefers Mele to Hasan as the origin of the Z2 invariant, and notes his own proximity to the band-theory side.
responses.response: I agree on stability and on Mele over Hasan, for the reason given above. He also discloses proximity to DFT and band theory, which makes his judgement on the calculational side of this case better informed than mine, and I defer to it there. I note that his alternatives, B051 and B018, show he counts B051 as serious. I do not read that as a conflict with my move.

uncertainties: Whether the citation wording can separate the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-symmetric edge states from the 2016 prize clearly enough for those who raised the overlap.
Whether omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, with Zhang deceased, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is acceptable under the three-name cap.
I rely on my own recollection of priority history in condensed matter, outside my field, and have not checked it against documents.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My field is string theory, gravity and cosmology, far from topological insulators, moire materials or atomic clocks. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any shortlisted candidate. My condensed-matter judgement is second-hand, and I disclose that limit again. No change from round 1.
